sentences.text: Guizhouichthyosaurus was a large ichthyosaur, typically about 5 meters long, with some specimens exceeding 6 meters.
Some reported specimens of Guizhouichthyosaurus reached a total length of around 7 meters.
Size estimates based on 86 presacral and 110 caudal vertebrae result in a total length of 10 meters.
Guizhouichthyosaurus had a long, powerful snout and a low sagittal crest on the back of its skull.
Guizhouichthyosaurus possessed a long and powerful snout.
The teeth of Guizhouichthyosaurus were conical with blunted tips and set in sockets.
Guizhouichthyosaurus had approximately 65 vertebrae before the hips and 2 hip vertebrae.
A specimen of Guizhouichthyosaurus contains the preserved torso and limbs of a thalattosaur named Xinpusaurus.
The gastroliths found in the specimen vary in size from 0.6 to 3.7 cm in diameter and are generally round.
Researchers found that the roughly 1 kilogram of gastroliths was insufficient to serve as ballast for an animal that could weigh as much as a ton.
A specimen of G. tangae preserves fish bones and bivalves in its stomach region, indicating it ate other prey besides large marine reptiles.
The genus Guizhouichthyosaurus was established by Cao and Luo in 2000.
Guizhouichthyosaurus likely used eel-like swimming, which was less efficient than the cod- or tuna-like swimming of later ichthyosaurs.
Triassic ichthyosaurs like Guizhouichthyosaurus likely used eel-like swimming, whereas later species evolved more efficient cod-like or tuna-like swimming styles.
A 2019 study used computational fluid dynamics to model the swimming energy demands of Guizhouichthyosaurus alongside eight other ichthyosaur taxa.
Guizhouichthyosaurus generated more drag than other studied ichthyosaurs due to its large flippers.
Guizhouichthyosaurus had small teeth without cutting edges, which were suitable for holding prey like cephalopods rather than cutting them.
Guizhouichthyosaurus was apparently a generalist feeder.
Guizhouichthyosaurus was a large ichthyosaur that fed by suction, helping it catch invertebrates, shell-less cephalopods, and fish with its narrow, completely toothless snout.
Guizhouichthyosaurus had an ecological niche similar to modern humpback whales, with reduced tail flippers and a relatively small head compared to its body.
Despite having small, smooth-edged teeth, Guizhouichthyosaurus was an apex predator capable of eating other large marine reptiles, as shown by a thalattosaur skeleton found in its stomach region.
Researchers hypothesized that the Guizhouichthyosaurus died soon after consuming its large prey.
A 2013 study divided well-preserved specimens of Guizhouichthyosaurus into two morphotypes, Type A and Type B, which researchers considered variations of the same species.
Researchers suggested the two morphotypes of Guizhouichthyosaurus likely represented sexual dimorphism rather than growth stages, as there was no significant size difference between them.
Researchers hypothesized that Type A individuals were females due to their longer trunks and shorter tails, a trait seen in modern lizards, though this was not confirmed by pregnant specimens.
Guizhouichthyosaurus is classified in the kingdom Animalia, phylum Chordata, class Sauropsida, order Ichthyosauria, and family Shastasauridae.
Guizhouichthyosaurus was previously reassigned to the genus Shastasaurus but is now considered a distinct genus.
A 2011 study by P. Martin Sander and colleagues concluded that Guizhouichthyosaurus was quite distinct from Shastasaurus.
Guizhouichthyosaurus lived during the Late Triassic period in southwest China.
Guizhouichthyosaurus lived during the early Carnian stage of the Late Triassic in southwestern China.
Guizhouichthyosaurus lived from the Ladinian to the Carnian stages, between 241.464 and 227.3 million years ago.
Fossils of Guizhouichthyosaurus have also been found in the Middle Triassic Zhuganpo Formation.
It is debated whether the species Callawayia wolonggangense belongs to Guizhouichthyosaurus, as recent studies found no traits unambiguously linking it to that genus.

It is debated whether the morphological differences between Type A and Type B Guizhouichthyosaurus represent sexual dimorphism, as no pregnant specimens exist to confirm the hypothesis that Type A are females.
It is debated whether the gastrolith clusters were stored by the animal or formed after death, with some researchers suggesting the stones may have killed the animal by clogging its intestines.
The function of gastroliths is controversial, with some suggesting buoyancy control, though researchers argue the stones were insufficient for ballast in a large animal.
